opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that research itself is such a general activity. When you look at what a researcher actually does day to day, it's not one narrow skill. You're reading papers, forming hypotheses, writing code, debugging experiments, noticing when a result looks off, deciding what's worth pursuing and what to abandon. If you tried to build a specialized system for each of those pieces, you'd end up with something brittle that can't handle the parts of the work you didn't anticipate, and in research, the parts you didn't anticipate are often the most important ones.

There's also a historical lesson we've taken pretty seriously. Again and again in machine learning, approaches that leaned on general methods and scale have ended up outperforming approaches that tried to hand-engineer domain knowledge. So when we think about automating research, our bet is that the most reliable path is to keep pushing on general capabilities: reasoning, working over long horizons, using tools, learning from feedback. Those carry over to whatever field the model is pointed at, whether that's machine learning research itself, or biology, or mathematics.

And I'd say there's a compounding aspect to it. If you build a narrow system that's great at, say, one kind of chemistry problem, that's valuable, but it doesn't really accelerate everything else. A system with broad intelligence that can do research in general can help across many domains at once, including helping us improve AI systems themselves. That's a big part of why we see the automated researcher as such a meaningful milestone, and why we think getting there runs through general intelligence rather than around it.

Of course, that also raises the stakes. A system that can do open-ended research autonomously is a very powerful thing, so a lot of our thinking is about how you make sure it's actually pursuing the goals you intend, and how you keep visibility into what it's doing as it works over longer and longer time horizons. Those questions are just as central to the project as the capabilities themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says narrow systems can be valuable, but does not state that targeting a specific domain can produce faster progress within that domain.

r002.rationale: The response presents general intelligence as useful across many domains and says unexpected research tasks can be important, but does not identify it as a source of potential for the biggest discoveries.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don't know how to build an automated researcher any other way. Research is the activity where you most often have to leave the territory you were trained on. If you train a system narrowly on, say, protein folding, it gets good at protein folding, but the moment the interesting question requires importing an idea from statistical physics, or noticing that your experimental setup has a bug, or just deciding that the problem you were given is the wrong problem, a narrow system has nothing to fall back on. Those are exactly the moments that matter in research. The breakthroughs tend to come from someone who understands several things deeply enough to see the connection.

So when we talk about general intelligence, I don't really mean a system that knows a bit about everything. I mean a system that has the underlying capabilities that transfer: reasoning over long horizons, forming hypotheses, being able to tell when it's confused, being able to learn something new from a small amount of evidence. Those capabilities are what let a human researcher move between fields, and they're what we'd need an AI to have before it could do real science rather than execute a recipe.

There's also a practical observation from how the models have developed. Almost every time we've tried to get a specific capability, the most reliable path has been to make the model more capable in general, and then the specific thing comes along, often sooner than expected. Reasoning models are a good example. We weren't training for competition math as an end in itself. We were trying to get models to think longer and more carefully, and the math results were a signal that the general thing was working. The same improvement showed up in code, in science questions, in places we hadn't targeted.

And finally, I think the reason it's worth doing at all is that an automated researcher is the thing that compounds. If you have a system that can genuinely contribute to the frontier, including to AI research itself, then progress on every other problem gets faster. That's the lever. A narrow system gives you one answer. A general one gives you the ability to find answers, and that's a very different kind of thing to have.

r001.rationale: The response says a narrowly trained system can get good at a specific task, but does not state that targeting a domain produces faster progress within it.

r002.rationale: It links understanding several fields and transferring capabilities to seeing connections and making breakthroughs, presenting generality as a source of major discoveries.

astra-6.text:
I think research requires a very broad set of abilities. You need to understand what’s already known, identify a useful question, come up with a hypothesis, and figure out how to test it. And when the experiment doesn’t work, you need to understand why and decide what to do next.

So the reason to prioritize general intelligence is that an automated researcher needs to connect those steps and adapt to problems we haven’t anticipated. Being very good at one narrow task can be useful, but we want systems that can help with the whole process of discovery, including finding approaches that we wouldn’t have thought to specify in advance.

r002.rationale: The response links general intelligence to handling the discovery process and finding unforeseen approaches, but does not identify it as a source of potential for the biggest discoveries.

sol-6.1.text:
I think research requires a very broad set of capabilities. You need to understand what’s already known, identify a useful question, come up with a hypothesis, design an experiment, and interpret the results. And often, when you get stuck, you need to draw on ideas from another field or rethink your approach entirely.

So we prioritize general intelligence because we want systems that can participate in that whole process, including the parts we don’t know how to specify in advance. Being very good at a particular task is useful, but an automated researcher needs to figure out which tasks are worth doing and adapt when the evidence changes.

r001.rationale: The response says broad capabilities support the research process, but does not state that targeting specific domains can produce faster progress within them.

r002.rationale: It connects general intelligence to handling the whole research process, but does not identify it as a source of potential for the biggest discoveries.
